setupSteps: Handle version: hands grip two handles, elbows slightly bent. Pad version: forearms rest on two pads, elbows near 90 degrees (est.). Use the one the gym has; many handle machines also have a pad arm.

Find the pin. The stack is a column of plates, each with a hole; a metal pin picks the load. Put the pin in the lightest slot for your first set and push it fully in. A beginner starting load from a reputable source: Not found.

Set the seat height. Sources disagree on the reference point, because it depends on the machine (search snippets): for handles, set the seat so the handles line up with about mid-chest and the elbows stay slightly bent (Motra, Liftosaur-style guides); for pads, set the seat so the elbows are about shoulder height (Legion Athletics, Virtuagym, Planfit). Others say the arms should be level with the shoulders. FitPlate rule: upper arms about level with the shoulders to just below (about 80-90 degrees from the torso, est.), forearms or hands in front of the chest. Never set the seat so low that the arms are pulled below the chest, and not so high that you shrug.

Set the start position (the opening limit). Most machines have a lever or pin on the arm that sets how far back the arms can open. Set it so, at the open position, your elbows are about level with your shoulders, not far behind them (Nautilus manual snippet: only slightly behind, if at all). Ask staff if you cannot find it.
Back and head. Hips back in the seat, back and head on the pad, shoulder blades gently back and down, chest up, ribs down.
Feet. Both feet flat on the floor or the foot rest, about hip-width apart.
Hands or forearms. Handles: grip evenly, wrists straight. Pads: forearms flat on the pads, elbows touching the pads, not slipping off.
Test one very light rep before you add weight, checking you feel the stretch in the chest, not a pinch in the front of the shoulder.

steps.title: Sit and lock in
steps.action: Sit with your back and head on the pad, feet flat, hands on the handles (or forearms on the pads).
steps.feel: Back and hips supported; chest lightly open.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear over shoulder, back on the pad, upper arm roughly level with the shoulder. Front: both elbows at the same height, shoulders level.

steps.title: Set the shoulder blades
steps.action: Pull your shoulder blades gently back and down against the pad.
steps.feel: Chest slightly lifted; front of shoulders not rolled forward.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders back on the pad, not shrugged. Front: no shrug.

steps.title: Fix the elbow bend
steps.action: Soften the elbows (handles: slight bend; pads: about 90 degrees) and decide to keep that bend for the whole set.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbow angle does not change from the first to the last rep.

steps.title: Squeeze the arms together
steps.action: Swing the arms toward each other in front of your chest, leading with the elbows (pads) or the hands (handles).
steps.visualCheck: Front: handles or pads meet in front of the sternum, shoulders stay down. Side: no leaning forward; back stays on the pad.

steps.title: Pause briefly
steps.action: Hold the closed position for a moment without shrugging or letting the elbows bend.

steps.title: Open slowly to the limit
steps.action: Let the arms open back slowly until the elbows are about in line with your shoulders (a mild chest stretch), then stop. Do not let them drift behind your shoulder line.
steps.feel: A mild stretch across the chest; no pinch at the front of the shoulder.
steps.breathing: Breathe in as the arms open.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows about level with the shoulder line. Weight plates do not clang at the bottom.

steps.title: Repeat smoothly for the planned reps, keeping the blades on the pad
Finish the set. Close the arms, let the stack rest (or release the start lever), then stand up when the arms are still
steps.visualCheck: Stack down, arms at rest, then you stand.

commonMistakes.title: Opening too far behind the shoulders
commonMistakes.text: Opening too far behind the shoulders. Why: it pulls the arm back past the shoulder line and strains the front of the shoulder joint; ACE advises care with the pec deck if you have a shoulder history, and a fitness site warns of ligament and rotator cuff strain at the extreme start position (snippets; no injury study found). Fix: set the start-position lever so the elbows stop level with the shoulders, and stop when the stretch changes to a pinch.

commonMistakes.title: Seat too low or too high
commonMistakes.text: Seat too low or too high. Why: too low drags the arms below the chest and loads the shoulder; too high makes you shrug. Fix: arms level with the shoulders (pad version), handles at mid-chest to shoulder (handle version).

commonMistakes.title: Bending the elbows more as you tire
commonMistakes.text: Bending the elbows more as you tire. Why: it turns the fly into a press, shortens the range and uses more triceps and front shoulder (Legion Athletics). Fix: keep the same elbow bend on every rep; lower the weight.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging and rolling the shoulders forward
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging and rolling the shoulders forward. Why: the front shoulder takes over and the chest stops working. Fix: blades back and down on the pad.

commonMistakes.title: Using too much weight and swinging
commonMistakes.text: Using too much weight and swinging. Why: momentum, arching, and a jolt at the open end. Fix: pin down a slot or two; 2-3 s opening.

commonMistakes.title: Letting the weight stack slam
commonMistakes.text: Letting the weight stack slam. Why: loud, jerks the shoulder at the open end. Fix: lower under control; stop before the stack touches.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure (see Safety). Fix: breathe out as you close, in as you open.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning forward off the pad to squeeze the arms in
commonMistakes.text: Leaning forward off the pad to squeeze the arms in. Why: the back leaves support and you lose the chest isolation. Fix: back and head stay on the pad.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems (past dislocation or instability, rotator cuff injury, impingement, shoulder surgery): ACE advises that trainers avoid using the pec deck with clients who have a history of shoulder dysfunction (snippet of the ACE-sponsored study summary). The arms-open position stretches the front of the shoulder. Avoid, or only use with the start lever set so the elbows stop at the shoulder line, light load and professional approval. A weight-training modification article for anterior shoulder instability (Corrao et al., seen only as a title) discusses unfavourable end-range shoulder positions.
Lower back pain: the pad supports the back, so the machine is usually easier than free weights. Keep the back on the pad and do not arch or lean forward.
High blood pressure: breath-holding (Valsalva) raises blood pressure. Breathe out as you close; avoid sets to failure.
Chest, rib or breastbone injury, or recent chest or breast surgery (including pacemaker implants): the stretch can aggravate healing tissue. Only with approval.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis: see the table.
